title: Tired of Cluttered Productivity Apps? This One’s Just a Text Document
gist: Tasks.txt, a free Mac app by Ukrainian programmer Yevhen Kharkivskyi built on Gina Trapani's todo.txt system, stores an entire to-do workflow in a couple of plain text files on the user's own machine with no account, cloud sync, telemetry or servers. The review frames local-first, zero-telemetry, non-subscription software as a rarity worth choosing precisely because mainstream productivity apps hold user data hostage to recurring revenue.

insights.claim: Tasks.txt stores a user's entire task list, archive and scratchpad in a couple of human-readable text documents on the local machine that can be opened in any text editor rather than in a cloud database.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Open, portable file formats eliminate switching costs, which is the structural threat to subscription productivity vendors whose moat is data lock-in.
insights.quote: Your task list isn't in some database in the cloud—it's on your computer, in an open, human-readable format.
insights.locator: All of this, notably, is stored in a couple of text documents

insights.claim: Tasks.txt is a free Mac app from Ukrainian programmer Yevhen Kharkivskyi built on the todo.txt system originally developed by Gina Trapani, showing a two-decade-old plain-text convention still supports shippable consumer products.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Durable open formats let independent developers build on top without platform permission, a low-cost distribution pattern worth watching in consumer software.
insights.locator: And that's what Tasks.txt, a totally free Mac app, offers

insights.claim: Because Tasks.txt data sits in open text files, a user can easily extract their tasks into another application later, making portability a feature rather than an afterthought.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Portability-as-a-feature is the emerging counter-positioning against incumbent SaaS; expect it to show up in more consumer tool marketing.
insights.locator: This simplicity means you can easily grab your tasks

insights.claim: The Tasks.txt website states there is no account, no cloud sync, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting and no servers, and that nothing leaves the user's machine.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: A total absence of data collection is now a marketable product claim, signaling consumer willingness to trade features for privacy.
insights.quote: There is no account, no cloud sync, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting,
insights.locator: And Tasks.txt makes it clear that your tasks are completely private

insights.claim: The reviewer argues that no-data-collection software is a rarity in an era when every piece of software is trying to hold user data hostage to sell a subscription, and that this alone makes Tasks.txt worth considering.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Backlash against data-hostage subscription models is becoming an explicit purchase driver, a demand-side risk to consumer SaaS retention.
insights.quote: This is a rarity in the modern age, where every piece of software is trying to hold your data hostage to sell a subscription.
insights.locator: And Tasks.txt makes it clear that your tasks are completely private

insights.claim: A reviewer who has spent decades testing to-do list applications concludes most of them are far too complicated because a to-do list is fundamentally just a list, a task humans handled on paper long before computers.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Feature escalation, including bolted-on AI integrations, may be reducing rather than increasing perceived value in the consumer productivity category.
insights.quote: And I think we can all admit that most of these apps are way too complicated.

insights.claim: The reviewer concedes that some users genuinely need due dates, recurring tasks, sharing features and even AI integration, but argues most only need the digital equivalent of a piece of paper.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Segments the market into a small power-user tier that sustains subscriptions and a large majority addressable by free minimal tools.
insights.locator: It's possible that you, a modern human

insights.claim: Tasks.txt organizes work into just three states — Done, Next and Backlog — with Done cleared into an archive at the start of each day, a deliberately minimal workflow model rather than a project-management hierarchy.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Shows the minimum viable structure users actually need, a benchmark against which bloated competitor roadmaps can be judged.
insights.locator: Open Tasks.txt and you'll see a simple list

insights.claim: Tasks.txt can be driven entirely from the keyboard, with the cursor already active in the entry box, Cmd+Enter to complete a task and Cmd+Up/Down to reorder, while remaining equally usable with a mouse.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Keyboard-complete interaction without forcing it is the execution detail that separates a usable minimal app from a gimmick.
insights.locator: It's possible to use this application using only the keyboard
